questions.skillExplanation: Identify the object physically located under the door and map it to the matching noun.
reasoningOperations: Inspect the object under the door.
Match its rectangular paper-mail form to the options.
questions.questionMechanism: The prepositional cue 'under the door' isolates one pictured object among nearby plant, sign, and umbrella distractors.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: All four option nouns are represented or plausible in the scene, so location is decisive.
questions.correctRationale: A flat addressed envelope is partly under the door; A is correct.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Meeting-room illustration shows an envelope lying under the door.

B.rationale: A plant appears beside the door, not under it.
B.misconceptionTarget: Naming a salient nearby object without using the preposition.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Plant is left of the door.

C.rationale: The Meeting Room sign hangs on the door.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Sign is mounted on the door.

D.rationale: The umbrella stands to the right of the door.
D.misconceptionTarget: Choosing another recognizable object in the picture.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Umbrella is in a stand beside the door.

studentFailureModes: Naming the most salient object instead of the one satisfying 'under'.
misconceptionsTargeted: Visual vocabulary questions often hinge on spatial language, not noun recognition alone.

shallowRecall.explanation: The visual location must be inspected.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Place several familiar objects around a landmark and make a preposition select exactly one.
simplificationConstraints: Preserve spatial cue and multiple pictured objects.
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Use two-step spatial relation such as between/behind.

questions.skillExplanation: Find the earliest time at which all four requested breads have become available.
reasoningOperations: Read each requested bread's oven time.
Take the latest of those four times and map it to the first feasible option.
questions.questionMechanism: Availability is a max-time constraint across white bread 10:30, bagels 11:30, challah 3:30, and farm bread 4:30.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: Earlier options become tempting if a learner forgets one family member's bread.
questions.correctRationale: Farm bread is the last required bread to come out at 4:30pm, so the earliest listed time after all four are available is 5:00pm; C is correct.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Baker's Kitchen schedule lists white bread 10:30am, bagels 11:30am, challah 3:30pm, farm bread 4:30pm.

A.rationale: 11:00 is before bagels, challah, and farm bread are all available.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Several requested breads appear later than 11:00.

B.rationale: 4:00 is still before farm bread at 4:30.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Farm bread: 4:30pm.

D.rationale: 7:00 works but is not the earliest possible listed time.
D.misconceptionTarget: Satisfying feasibility without optimizing earliest time.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: All requested breads are already available by 5:00pm.

studentFailureModes: Failing to combine all four family constraints.
Choosing any feasible time rather than the earliest.
misconceptionsTargeted: Earliest-all-available questions require taking the latest prerequisite time.

shallowRecall.explanation: Multiple schedule entries must be integrated.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Use a schedule and several simultaneous requirements so the answer is the maximum prerequisite time.
simplificationConstraints: Keep at least three requested items with distinct times.

evidenceReferences.quoteOrDescription: Bakery timetable provides all prerequisite times.

questions.skillExplanation: Check each statement against bakery hours, discounts, day restrictions, and membership terms.
reasoningOperations: Test each option's quantity, day, or timing claim.
questions.questionMechanism: Only the half-price timing statement matches both weekday and weekend closing hours.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: Distractors each alter one precise visual detail: days open, weekend availability, or membership amount.
questions.correctRationale: Bread is half price after 8pm on weekdays and after 7pm on weekends, exactly one hour before the respective 9pm and 8pm closing times; B is correct.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Half-price after 8pm, after 7pm weekends; business hours close at 9pm weekdays and 8pm weekends.

A.rationale: The bakery is open seven days, not five.
A.misconceptionTarget: Reading Mon-Fri and overlooking Sat-Sun hours.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Business hours list weekdays and weekends.

C.rationale: Croissants and pretzels are marked Friday only, not weekends.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Both items carry Friday-only notation.

D.rationale: Membership costs $100 and saves 10%; it does not save $100 on Fridays.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: $100 membership fee; 10% savings on all shopping.

studentFailureModes: Matching a familiar number without its label.
misconceptionsTargeted: Multi-field visual documents require exact label-value binding.

shallowRecall.explanation: Several document regions must be cross-checked.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Place related numeric facts in separate regions and build distractors by swapping their roles.

evidenceReferences.quoteOrDescription: Schedule, pricing, membership and hours jointly support the choice.

questions.skillExplanation: Identify which transport choice the festival information positively recommends while rejecting prohibited alternatives.
reasoningOperations: Separate invitations from closures and unavailable parking.
questions.questionMechanism: The notice explicitly welcomes visitors to use the free festival bus, while two distractors conflict with closure rules.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: The correct option is supported as a recommendation, not merely as a possible route.
questions.correctRationale: The notice explicitly welcomes visitors to take the Free Festival Bus from Goat Street Station; A is correct.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Information item 2 welcomes visitors to take the Free Festival Bus.

B.rationale: The festival runs April 1 to May 31; weekends are not recommended over weekdays.
B.misconceptionTarget: Assuming events are best on weekends.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: No weekend preference is stated.

C.rationale: Fox Street is closed during the festival.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Item 4 says Fox Street is closed.

D.rationale: Garden Square is unavailable for car parking because it hosts the farmers' market.
D.misconceptionTarget: Using a prominent nearby place without checking its rule.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Item 5 says Garden Square won't be open for car parking.

misconceptionsTargeted: A recommended action requires positive source support, not mere feasibility.

shallowRecall.explanation: Notice rules must be compared with each scenario.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Mix one explicitly encouraged route with plausible but prohibited alternatives in a map notice.
simplificationConstraints: Preserve explicit recommendation and conflicting rules.
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Require combining transport and time constraints.

evidenceReferences.quoteOrDescription: Festival notice and map ground the recommendation.

questions.skillExplanation: Use the map's transit symbols, streets, and block layout to verify a claim about the farmers' market.
reasoningOperations: Compare nearby metro stations, bus stops, blocks, and flower market.
questions.questionMechanism: Correctness depends on comparing map distances rather than reading a single label.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: Every distractor uses real locations or transit numbers but misbinds proximity or street placement.
questions.correctRationale: The Koala Street metro station sits immediately next to Garden Square, making it the nearest metro station to the farmers' market; D is correct.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Garden Square is beside Koala Street, with a metro symbol directly adjacent.

A.rationale: The flower market is across Lion Road and offset from Garden Square, not simply next to it.
A.misconceptionTarget: Treating nearby named places as adjacent.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Faun's Weekend Flower Market and Garden Square occupy different blocks.

B.rationale: Satyr's Park and Garden Square are separated into different blocks by Lion Road/Puppy Street geometry.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Festival park and farmers' market are not on one block.

C.rationale: Bus 157 serves the stop by Koala/Goat-side area, not the Puppy Street stop shown by Garden Square's east side.
C.misconceptionTarget: Binding a route number to the wrong stop.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Puppy Street stop lists 28, 125, 505, not 157.

studentFailureModes: Using only landmark names without checking road boundaries.
Reading a bus number from the wrong stop.

shallowRecall.explanation: Multiple spatial relations must be compared.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Use a transit map where distractors preserve real labels but attach them to wrong positions.
simplificationConstraints: Keep multiple transit nodes and road boundaries.
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Ask for a route requiring transfer between modes.

evidenceReferences.quoteOrDescription: Map geometry and station symbols are decisive.

questions.skillExplanation: Infer the hosts’ shared social flaw by interpreting the guests’ sarcastic responses across both anecdotes.
reasoningOperations: Interpret the dry jokes in both stories.
Abstract the common criticism of Yan and Chang.
questions.questionMechanism: Both anecdotes indirectly criticize stinginess through hyperbolic sarcasm.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: The trait is never named; it must be recovered from pragmatic intent across parallel stories.
questions.correctRationale: Yan has a good life yet serves only a tiny fish, while Chang owns many animals yet claims there is no lunch; both friends mock their unwillingness to share, so B is correct.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Yan serves one tiny fish; Chang refuses lunch despite keeping many ducks and chickens; each guest responds sarcastically.

A.rationale: Food appears in both stories, but the jokes criticize withholding food rather than enjoying it.
A.misconceptionTarget: Choosing a repeated topic instead of the inferred trait.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Guests point out the mismatch between resources and hospitality.

C.rationale: Having visitors does not show the hosts like making friends; their poor hospitality is the focus.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The guests use criticism, not praise.

D.rationale: No resistance to novelty appears in either story.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The conflict is sharing food/resources.

studentFailureModes: Focusing on food as topic instead of hospitality as social behavior.
misconceptionsTargeted: Pragmatic meaning often lies in why a speaker says an absurd thing.

shallowRecall.explanation: Two stories and their sarcastic punchlines must be integrated.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Pair two short anecdotes with parallel sarcasm so learners infer an unstated shared trait.
simplificationConstraints: Preserve resource abundance, withholding, and sarcastic response.
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Make one criticism subtler and require comparison.

questions.skillExplanation: Compare the start of shaded social-distancing periods across four city charts.
reasoningOperations: Use the legend to identify shaded social-distancing time.
Compare the left edge of shading across Portland, New York, Denver, and Pittsburgh.
questions.questionMechanism: One city clearly begins the shaded intervention earlier than the other three.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: The learner must interpret the legend and align four common x-axes rather than rely on death totals.
questions.correctRationale: New York's shaded social-distancing period begins earliest on the shared week axis, so B is correct.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Four-city chart shows New York shading beginning around week 3, earlier than the other cities.

A.rationale: Portland has a long/intermittent shaded period but does not start first.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Portland shading starts later than New York's.

C.rationale: Denver starts later and has two shaded periods.
C.misconceptionTarget: Mistaking multiple interventions for earliest intervention.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Denver's first shaded block begins after New York's.

D.rationale: Pittsburgh has the largest 24-week death total and a later intervention start; neither supports earliest.
D.misconceptionTarget: Using outcome magnitude instead of intervention timing.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Pittsburgh shading begins after New York's.

studentFailureModes: Comparing death curves or totals instead of shading start times.
misconceptionsTargeted: Chart questions require matching the asked variable to the correct visual encoding.

shallowRecall.explanation: Four visual panels must be compared using the legend.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Use small multiples with a shared axis and ask for a timing comparison encoded by background shading.
simplificationConstraints: Keep legend and common time axis.
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Ask learners to combine start time with outcome to infer a pattern.

evidenceReferences.quoteOrDescription: Shaded intervention periods across four city panels.
